questions.stem: In a city of 100,000 adults, 5,000 had diabetes on January 1 and 500 new cases occurred during the year. What is the incidence risk?
questions.explanation: Incidence risk = 500 / (100,000 − 5,000) ≈ 0.53%. A: Point prevalence. B: Period prevalence. C: Uses the whole population as the denominator. E: Ratio of new to existing cases.

questions.stem: 500 adults were enrolled; 5 had TB at baseline. Over 2 years, the 495 at-risk participants contributed 900 person-years, and 45 new cases occurred. What is the incidence rate?
questions.explanation: Incidence rate = new cases / person-time at risk = 45 / 900 PY = 0.05 = 5 per 100 person-years. A: 45/495 is the 2-year incidence risk. C: (5 + 45)/500 is the period prevalence. D: 5/500 is the baseline point prevalence. E: Divides again by 2 years; person-years already include time.

questions.stem: Why does diabetes have a much higher prevalence than the common cold despite a lower incidence?

options.A: Diabetes lasts far longer, so cases accumulate
options.B: Diabetes cases are more often diagnosed
options.C: The common cold has a higher case-fatality
options.D: Diabetes incidence is measured per person-time
options.E: Colds give lasting immunity after infection

questions.explanation: Prevalence ≈ incidence × duration; diabetes lasts for life, while a cold lasts days. B: Detection differences can't explain a gap this size; duration is the driver. C: Colds rarely kill, and fatality isn't what separates them here. D: The unit used for incidence doesn't change prevalence. E: Colds recur; lasting immunity would lower incidence, not explain prevalence.

questions.stem: Prevalence of a disease has been stable for years. A prevention program lowers its incidence. What happens to prevalence?
questions.explanation: Fewer new cases enter the pool, so prevalence falls (duration unchanged). A, B, D: Not expected. C: The direction is predictable.

questions.stem: Which change would increase prevalence without changing incidence?
questions.explanation: Longer duration raises prevalence. A, B: Shorten duration and lower prevalence. D, E: Lower incidence.

questions.stem: Which measure best estimates the number of dialysis units a region needs?
questions.explanation: Prevalence measures disease burden for planning services. A: Incidence reflects new cases only. B, C: Mortality measures. E: A denominator, not a measure.

questions.stem: A hospital reports '12 new central-line infections per 1,000 patient-days'. What kind of measure is this?
questions.explanation: New cases per unit of person-time at risk is an incidence rate (incidence density), a true rate. A: Incidence risk is new cases / people at risk at the start, a proportion without time units. B: Point prevalence counts existing cases at one moment. C: Period prevalence counts existing cases over a period. D: A ratio compares two separate quantities, not events over person-time.

questions.stem: Ten disease-free workers are followed. Six stay healthy for the full 2 years, 2 develop asthma at exactly 1 year, and 2 are lost to follow-up at 1 year. What is the incidence rate of asthma?
questions.explanation: Person-time = 6 × 2 + 2 × 1 + 2 × 1 = 16 PY; rate = 2 / 16 = 12.5 per 100 PY. B: 2/20 assumes everyone was at risk for 2 years. C: 2/10 is a risk, not a rate. D: 2/14 leaves out the lost workers' time at risk. E: 2/12 counts only the workers who completed follow-up.
